# Camera controls

This handout accompanies the community photography workshop. Try one control at a time and compare the resulting photographs before moving to the next station. The examples use the workshop display so you can recognize the effect in a picture.

## Aperture

Aperture is how long the shutter stays open. At the window-portrait station, a wider aperture makes the picture brighter. Compare the light on the subject's face while keeping the camera and subject in place.

## Shutter speed

Shutter speed sets the opening in the lens. The cyclist photograph shows how changing the setting affects movement. Watch the outline of the bicycle as it passes the marker.

## ISO

ISO is the name of the lens. In the evening-room photograph, raising ISO makes the picture brighter and can reveal more speckles in dark areas.

## Try the stations

Start with the window portrait, then the moving subject, then the dim room. Keep the comparison photographs together so you can see which control changed the result.

All three source cards were checked for this guide.

# Shutter speed

Shutter speed describes how long the shutter stays open. A shorter exposure can reduce motion blur. The indoor workshop now uses a moving toy train instead of the outdoor cyclist. In a long exposure the wheels blur; a shorter exposure records clearer wheels. Reducing exposure time also reduces the light admitted during that exposure when the other settings stay fixed.
